doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Studio guitars and amps; the Dinning Sisters session
summary: Gibson ES 175 and 335, miking the amp, and a quiet Twin amp on a session with Ginger Dinning.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Did the producers like a certain kind of guitar? I mean did they want you on a Strat or did they get that specific?
That, I’ve never been questioned on, as far as meaning when you went into the studio if you were a guitar player and I would bring a 175, ES 175 —

A Gibson ES 175, Epiphone, I have the Epiphone also, and then I would bring a 335, which is a Gibson also. That I find the most, the best recording guitar was the 335. That’s what Eric Clapton uses a lot. A 335. It’s a great guitar. It’s all around. But acoustic wise of course not, not for acoustic.
Did they used to put mics in front of your amp or you went direct into the —

A lot of them were the microphones in the beginning because they didn’t even have the XLR’s coming out in the back on all amplifiers. That was always high impedance and then that was noisy. But usually a mic in the front of the amp. I had a Twin amp, one of the first, I think 1958 or ’59, I don’t know when they first came out. They didn’t have reverb on it. And I did a recording session with The Dinning Sisters. Now I know there’s someone you never heard of.

Ginger was her name and she broke away from her two sisters and it was just myself and her and I brought this amp in and they put the mic in the front and he said it was the quietest amp he ever heard, the engineer, which was — because usually they always have a hiss or a hum, but that amp was quiet and I sold that amp. I’m sorry I ever sold that amp many years ago. I wish I still had it.
